passage: At the chai stall outside the Gurugram metro, Seema caught up with her friend Ujjwal after his first week at the new internship. "So, did you like it?" she asked. "Yeah. It was fine." Seema waited. Nothing else came. She tried again. "Okay, but what was it like walking in on the first day?" Ujjwal laughed and put down his cup. "Honestly? Terrifying. Everyone was in suits and I was in a checked shirt. My manager called me by the wrong name for two days. And then on Thursday, she asked for my idea in a meeting, and they actually used it." He talked for twenty minutes: the canteen, the lift that stopped on every floor, the colleague who lent him a charger. Walking home, Seema thought about it. "Did you like it?" had got one word. "What was it like?" had got a story.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal wearing on his first day?
qa.a: A checked shirt.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling as he described his first week?
qa.a: He felt a mix of fear and pride, calling the first day terrifying but lighting up when his idea was used.

qa.q: Why did Seema's second question work better?
qa.a: It was open and curious, asking what the day was like instead of a yes-or-no question, so Ujjwal could tell a full story.

qa.q: What would change if Seema had stopped after 'Did you like it?'
qa.a: She would have heard only 'fine' and missed the fear, the wrong name and the idea that got used.

grounding: Shows a young adult switching from a closed question to an open one and getting a much fuller answer from a friend.

passage:
"Nikita! You're back from the trek! Did you have fun?"
"Yeah, it was good."
Damini waited. "Just good?"
"Mm."
Damini tried again. "What was the hardest part?"
Nikita paused. "The last climb. It was so steep, I nearly turned back. I cried a bit, actually."
"Really? What made you keep going?"
"There was this old man in our group, like sixty-five, who just kept saying, 'Chhota kadam, chhota kadam.' Small steps. So I did."
"And what was it like at the top?"
Nikita's face lit up. "Quiet. Like, totally quiet. I sat there and felt like my brain finally switched off."
Damini grinned. "That's way more than 'good.'"
"You asked better questions," Nikita laughed.

qa.q: What did the old man in Nikita's group keep saying?
qa.a: 'Chhota kadam, chhota kadam.' Small steps.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling at the top of the climb?
qa.a: Nikita felt calm and peaceful, as if the brain had finally switched off.

qa.q: What made Damini's later questions work better than 'Did you have fun?'
qa.a: They were open and specific, like 'What was the hardest part?', inviting Nikita to tell a story instead of just agreeing.

qa.q: What would change if Damini had accepted 'it was good'?
qa.a: Damini would never have heard about the steep climb, the old man's 'small steps' or the quiet at the top.

grounding: Shows a young adult using open, curious questions to get a friend's full story instead of one-word answers.

passage:
After Ritu's dance audition, I used to ask, "Did it go well?" She'd say, "Yeah, I think so," and that was it. I thought she just didn't want to talk.
Then my cousin, who's a counsellor, told me I was asking questions that only needed a yes. So after Ritu's next audition, I tried something different. "What was it like, being up there?"
She sat down on my bed. "My legs were shaking. But when the music started, I forgot everyone. Except one judge who kept yawning. That made me so angry I danced harder." She laughed. "I think it was my best ever."
She talked for almost an hour. I'd never heard any of that before.
I'm Rehana. I still catch myself asking yes-or-no questions. But now I notice.

qa.q: What did one judge keep doing during Ritu's audition?
qa.a: The judge kept yawning.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel during the audition?
qa.a: Her legs were shaking with nerves at first, then she felt angry at the yawning judge and danced harder, feeling it was her best ever.

qa.q: What small change did Rehana make, and why did it help?
qa.a: Rehana asked 'What was it like?' instead of 'Did it go well?', which invited Ritu to tell a real story.

qa.q: What would change if Rehana kept asking yes-or-no questions?
qa.a: Ritu would probably keep answering 'yeah, I think so', and Rehana would miss the real stories.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning that open, curious questions invite a friend's full story while closed ones invite a short yes.

passage: The storm had shut the highway, the warehouse was flooded to the ankles, and the shipment to Delhi was a day late. Binita had made a call at 6 am: hold the trucks until the road reopened. At nine, her manager Indu arrived, wet and tense. "Why did you hold the trucks? What were you thinking? Who told you to decide that? Do you know what the client will say?" Binita felt her chest tighten. Every question sounded like an accusation. She mumbled, "I thought it was safer," and stopped talking. Indu went to her office. An hour later she came back with two cups of tea. "Sorry, Binita. I was panicking. Can you walk me through how you decided?" Binita breathed out. She explained the road closure, the driver's call, the flooded bridge. Indu listened. "That was the right call," she said.

qa.q: What time did Binita decide to hold the trucks?
qa.a: At 6 am.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when Indu fired questions at her?
qa.a: She felt attacked and tense, her chest tightening, so she mumbled one line and stopped talking.

qa.q: What changed when Indu came back with tea?
qa.a: Indu apologised and asked the same thing with a softer tone and real curiosity, so Binita could explain clearly.

qa.q: How did Indu feel when she first arrived?
qa.a: Indu was panicking and tense, worried about the client and the delay.

Tarun's face changed. "Oh, Ayesha. I didn't know."
"You didn't ask like that before."
"I'm asking now. What do you need?"

passage:
I sat across from Reena at the planning meeting for the new school-meal programme in our district. Everyone was excited. Vandana, the senior project lead, had just presented the timeline, and the room was nodding.
Then Reena, who'd joined only three months ago, raised her hand. "Can I ask something? What could make this plan fail?" A few people frowned. Vandana paused. Then she said, slowly, "If the kitchens don't get gas cylinders on time in the monsoon."
The room went quiet. Nobody had planned for that. Someone added, "And if the drivers can't reach the hill schools." For the next half hour, the whole team listed risks and fixes.
I don't know if Reena was nervous. She didn't look it. But after the meeting Vandana stopped by her desk and said, "Keep asking that question."

qa.q: What was the meeting planning?
qa.a: The new school-meal programme in the district.

qa.q: How did Vandana seem to feel about Reena's question by the end?
qa.a: Vandana seemed grateful and impressed, telling Reena to keep asking that question.

qa.q: Why did Reena's question help the team?
qa.a: Asking what would make the plan fail surfaced hidden risks, like gas cylinders in the monsoon, so the team could plan fixes.

qa.q: How might the people who frowned at first see Reena's question later?
qa.a: They would probably see it as useful, since it led to a half hour of important planning.

grounding: Shows a thoughtful colleague asking what would make a plan fail, surfacing hidden risks and showing respect for others' views.

Wednesday: Tanvir came back with a list. "Your plan assumes riders have smartphones with good data. In the outer areas, half don't. And the festival week is when most riders go home." Manoj's stomach dropped. Then he thanked him. They added a phone-call option and moved the launch by a week.
Two weeks later: The launch went smoothly. A rival app launched during the festival and crashed. The director asked Manoj how he'd known. "I asked Tanvir what I was missing," he said.

passage:
"Mridul, you're so pleased with your design, I can see it," said Aparna aunty, smiling. "Let me tell you about my first bridge. I was twenty-five, a junior engineer in the PWD. My design for a small river bridge near Satara was beautiful. I was proud. At the review, my senior, Mr. Kulkarni, asked only one question: 'What could make this fail?'
I was offended. Then I thought about it. The monsoon floods. Tree trunks coming down the river. My pillars were too close together. A big log could jam there and push the whole thing.
I went back and widened the gap. Two years later, a flood came with half a forest in it. The bridge held.
So before you show anyone, ask yourself that question. And ask someone who'll tell you the truth."

qa.a: Twenty-five.

qa.a: He probably saw talent but wanted her to check for hidden risks, respecting her enough to ask.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how being asked what would make her design fail surfaced a hidden risk and changed the outcome.

passage:
Badminton coach's note, Saturday.
Usha (10) lost her match in the under-12 district round. She came off the court in tears. Her father, Mr. Asif, said, "Arre, it's only a game. Stop crying, everyone is looking." Usha wiped her face fast and said, "I'm fine." She sat very straight and didn't cry again. But she didn't eat her snack, and she didn't speak on the drive to the next venue.
I spoke to Usha privately before the next match. I told her it was okay to be upset, that it meant she cared, and that she'd played a brave third set. She cried properly then, quietly, for a minute. Then she said, "I thought I wasn't allowed."
I also spoke to Mr. Asif. He listened and said he hadn't meant to shut her down.

qa.q: What did Mr. Asif say when Usha came off the court?
qa.a: He said, 'Arre, it's only a game. Stop crying, everyone is looking.'

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when she said 'I'm fine'?
qa.a: She felt hurt and ashamed of crying, so she hid her sadness even though she was still upset.

qa.q: What did the coach do next that helped Usha?
qa.a: The coach spoke to her privately, told her being upset showed she cared, praised her effort, and later spoke to her father.

qa.q: How did Mr. Asif respond when the coach spoke to him?
qa.a: He listened and said he hadn't meant to shut her down, which suggests he felt a little regretful.

grounding: Shows a child crying over a lost match told it's just a game, and learning to hide feelings rather than that they are small.

passage:
Sunday night
Lost the chess final today. I was so close. I cried in the corridor after, and my cousin Zeenat said, "Arre, it's just a game, Vasudha. Stop being a baby."
So I stopped. In front of everyone, I smiled and shook hands. At lunch I said, "It doesn't matter." But inside it mattered SO much. I'd practised every evening for three months.
I'm writing it here because I can't say it out loud anymore. I feel like if I show I'm sad, people will think I'm silly.
Nani called tonight. She asked, "How do you feel, really?" and I started crying again on the phone. She said, "Of course you're sad. You worked so hard." That helped.
Vasudha

qa.a: Every evening for three months.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel after Zeenat said 'Stop being a baby'?
qa.a: Vasudha felt hurt and silly for showing sadness, so the feelings got hidden behind a smile.

grounding: Shows a child crying over a lost match being told it's just a game, and learning to hide feelings rather than that they are small.

passage:
"You want to know what I learned this year? I'm Tejas, and this is about my friend Manjula.
Her father had a stroke in March. She called me that night, crying. My brain went straight to fixing. Which hospital? Did they try physiotherapy? Should she take leave?
She went quiet. Then she said, 'I just needed someone to hear me.'
I felt terrible. So the next time she called, I tried something else. I said, 'That sounds really, really hard.' And then, 'Do you want ideas, or just company right now?'
She said, 'Company.' So I just stayed on the phone. We didn't say much. A week later, she said, 'Now I want ideas.' And then my list actually helped.
It's such a small thing. Feel first. Then ask before fixing."

qa.q: When did Manjula's father have a stroke?
qa.a: In March.

passage:
I share an office with Jahnavi and Ganga, so I hear a lot. On Thursday, Ganga came back from a meeting and sat down heavily. "The client rejected the whole design. Three months of work."
I watched Jahnavi turn her chair. She didn't say "It's not so bad" or "Here's what to do." She said, "Ganga, that sounds really hard. Three months." Ganga nodded, eyes wet. Then Jahnavi asked, "Do you want ideas right now, or just company for a bit?"
Ganga laughed shakily. "Company. And tea."
They went to the pantry together. Twenty minutes later, I heard Ganga say, "Okay. Now I want ideas." Jahnavi pulled out a notebook.
I don't know what Ganga was feeling inside. But she looked lighter walking back to her desk.

qa.q: How long had Ganga worked on the rejected design?
qa.a: Three months.

qa.q: How did Ganga seem to feel after Jahnavi's question?
qa.a: She seemed relieved and a little lighter, laughing shakily and asking for company and tea.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi's approach work?
qa.a: She validated the feeling first and then asked permission before offering ideas, respecting Ganga's choice.

qa.q: What would change if Jahnavi had said 'It's not so bad'?
qa.a: Ganga might have felt dismissed and kept her feelings to herself.

grounding: Shows an observer watching a colleague validate first and then ask whether a friend wants ideas or company.

passage:
Tuesday: Varun called Lalit from the bus stop. "They laid me off. The whole team." Lalit's first instinct was to list job sites. Instead he said, "Varun, that sounds really hard. I'm so sorry." Then, "Do you want ideas right now, or just company?" Varun said, "Company." Lalit took an auto to his flat, and they watched cricket without talking much.
Friday: Varun messaged: "Okay. I think I want ideas now." Lalit came over with his laptop. They updated Varun's CV together and made a list of five companies.
The next Tuesday: Varun had two interviews lined up. "You know what helped most?" he said. "That first night, you didn't try to fix me."

qa.q: How many companies were on Varun and Lalit's list?
qa.a: Five companies.

qa.q: How did Varun feel on the night he was laid off?
qa.a: He was shocked and hurt, and wanted company more than advice.

qa.q: What made Lalit's support work?
qa.a: He validated first, asked whether Varun wanted ideas or company, and waited for Varun to ask before problem-solving.

qa.a: Varun might have felt rushed and unheard on a painful night, and been less ready for ideas later.

grounding: Shows a person validating a friend's hard news and asking permission before problem-solving, respecting feeling and choice.

passage:
Last Sunday, Aparna and I were playing snakes and ladders at her house, and we had the biggest fight. She said if you land on a ladder with a six, you get another turn. I said no, you don't. "Yes, you do!" "No, you DON'T!" We got louder and louder, saying the same thing again and again. Her mother came in.
She said, "Swati, before you answer, tell me what Aparna said." I was annoyed. "She said you get another turn." "Aparna, what did Swati say?" "That you don't." Then Aunty asked, "Why do you each think so?"
Aparna said her Nani plays that way. I said my book says no. Then we just decided to play Nani's way at Aparna's house, and the book way at mine.
I'm still not sure who's right. But we stopped shouting.

qa.q: What game were Swati and Aparna playing?
qa.a: Snakes and ladders.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling when asked to repeat what Aparna said?
qa.a: Swati felt annoyed at first, wanting to win the argument.

qa.q: What small step changed the argument?
qa.a: Saying back what the other person said before answering, and asking why each thought so, which helped them understand each other.

qa.q: How might Aparna have felt when Swati repeated her point?
qa.a: Aparna probably felt heard, which made it easier to explain her Nani's rule calmly.

grounding: Shows children arguing over a game by repeating their claims louder, and stating the other's view first starting to change the pattern.

passage:
Class 5 teacher's note, Wednesday.
At break, Vidya and Pranav were shouting over a cricket game. "You were OUT!" "I was NOT out!" Twelve times at least, each louder. Neither was listening.
I stepped in and made a rule: before you answer, you have to say what the other person just said. Pranav rolled his eyes. "She thinks I was out because the ball hit the stumps." Vidya said, "He thinks he wasn't out because the bail didn't fall." They both paused. Then Pranav said, "Oh. That's actually the real question."
They asked the PE teacher, who said the bail must fall. Vidya accepted it. I'll teach the "say it back" rule to the whole class on Friday.

qa.q: What did the PE teacher say about the bail?
qa.a: The bail must fall for a batter to be out.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when he realised the real question?
qa.a: He seemed surprised and more open, no longer just angry, once he heard Vidya's point clearly.

qa.q: What did the teacher's rule change, and why?
qa.a: Saying back what the other said forced them to listen, which showed them the real disagreement about the bail.

qa.q: How did Vidya respond to the PE teacher's answer?
qa.a: She accepted it, which suggests she felt the argument had been fair.

grounding: Shows children arguing louder over a game until stating what the other said helps them understand each other.

passage:
Tuesday
Sangeeta and I had a huge fight over hopscotch today. She said I stepped on the line. I said I didn't. We kept shouting "You did!" "I didn't!" until Didi came out and said we sounded like two crows.
Then Didi told us a trick: before you answer, say back what the other one said. I didn't want to. But I said, "Sangeeta says my foot touched the line." She said, "Trisha says her foot was inside." Then I said, "Maybe my toe touched it. Just a little."
Sangeeta laughed. "Okay, maybe just a little." We decided to redo my turn.
It was so weird. When I said her words, I stopped wanting to win so much.
Trisha

qa.q: What did Didi say they sounded like?
qa.a: Two crows.

qa.q: How did Trisha feel after saying Sangeeta's words?
qa.a: Trisha felt less stubborn, no longer wanting to win so much.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Saying back what the other person said worked, because it made both girls listen and admit a little.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta respond when Trisha admitted her toe touched?
qa.a: She laughed and admitted 'maybe just a little', agreeing to redo the turn.

grounding: Shows children arguing louder over a game until repeating the other's view helps them understand and settle it.

passage:
Monday: Lalit and his sister Hafsa fought over the family laptop. "You ALWAYS take it! You NEVER let me use it! Just like last year when you broke my headphones and never said sorry!" Hafsa shouted back, "And you always leave your socks everywhere!" Doors slammed.
Wednesday: Their Abbu sat them down. "Lalit, what exactly do you need?" Lalit thought. "The laptop on Thursday from six to eight, for my project."
Thursday: Lalit said to Hafsa, calmly, "Can I have the laptop from six to eight today? My project's due Friday." Hafsa blinked. "Oh. Sure. I'll use it after." It took ten seconds.

qa.q: When did Lalit need the laptop?
qa.a: Thursday from six to eight, for his project.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling during Monday's fight?
qa.a: He felt angry and frustrated, using 'always' and 'never' and dragging in old grievances.

qa.q: What changed on Thursday that made the argument solvable?
qa.a: Lalit asked for something specific and present, the laptop from six to eight, instead of using absolutes.

qa.q: How did Hafsa respond on Monday compared to Thursday?
qa.a: On Monday she fought back with her own complaint; on Thursday she agreed easily.

grounding: Shows a teenager escalating a quarrel with 'always' and 'never' and old grievances, and a specific present request making it solvable.

passage:
"Mridul, you said 'you never listen' to your mother just now. I heard," said Rashmi bua gently. "Sit. When I was sixteen, I said that to my mother every week. 'You never trust me. You always take Didi's side. Remember in Class 6 when you...' I'd drag up everything.
Every time, she'd get defensive. 'Never? What about last Tuesday?' And we'd fight about the word 'never' instead of the real problem.
Then my Nani told me: 'Say one thing that happened today. Only today.' So next time, I said, 'Amma, when you checked my phone this morning, I felt you don't trust me.' Amma stopped. She said, 'I was worried about a message.' We actually talked.
So try it, beta. Not 'never.' Just today."

qa.a: She felt unheard and angry, using 'never' and 'always' and dragging up old grievances.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Rashmi bua's story?

qa.q: How did Rashmi's mother respond to the specific complaint?
qa.a: She stopped and explained she was worried about a message, so they actually talked.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how 'always' and 'never' and old grievances made fights worse, and specific present issues kept them solvable.

passage: The rain had stopped the cricket match, and Samir and Chetan were stuck under the pavilion roof with nothing to do but fight. "You always hog the batting. You never pass the ball. Just like the tournament last year when you didn't let me bowl once!" Samir shouted. Chetan went red. "That's not true! And you always sulk when you're out early!" Other boys started watching. Samir's anger was loud, but even he could hear it wasn't going anywhere. He took a breath. "Okay. Forget always. Today, you batted for twelve overs and I got two. I want to open next innings." Chetan paused. "...Fine. Today that's fair." When the rain stopped, Samir opened. They didn't mention last year again.

qa.a: He felt angry and frustrated, using 'always' and 'never' and bringing up last year's tournament.

qa.q: What did Samir do that made the argument solvable?
qa.a: He dropped 'always' and stated a specific present issue, twelve overs to two, with a clear request.

qa.q: How did Chetan respond to the absolute accusations?
qa.a: He went red and got defensive, firing back with his own 'always'.

grounding: Shows a teenager escalating a quarrel with absolutes and old grievances, then switching to a specific present issue that makes it solvable.
